objectives: Reason about grain boundaries + grain size.

slides.title: Real crystals: defects everywhere
slides.body:
Perfect crystals exist only in textbooks. Real materials have **defects** at all length scales. Defects are NOT failures — they're features that determine most material properties.

**Point defects** (0-dimensional):
- **Vacancy**: empty lattice site. Equilibrium concentration depends on temperature: $n_v/N \approx \exp(-E_v/kT)$ where $E_v \sim 1$ eV.
- **Interstitial**: atom in a non-lattice site (small atoms like H, C, N).
- **Substitutional impurity**: foreign atom replacing a host atom.
- **Frenkel pair**: vacancy + interstitial (atom displaced).
- **Schottky defect**: vacancy pair in ionic crystals (preserves charge neutrality).

Vacancies enable atomic diffusion (atoms hop into them). Critical for diffusion-controlled phenomena: oxidation, creep, sintering, heat treatment.

**Line defects (1D): dislocations**:
- **Edge dislocation**: extra half-plane of atoms inserted into the crystal. Visualized as a 'wedge'.
- **Screw dislocation**: lattice planes spiraled around an axis like a ramp.
- **Mixed**: most real dislocations.

Dislocations are characterized by **Burgers vector** $\mathbf{b}$: the closure failure of a circuit around the dislocation.

**Why dislocations matter**: plastic deformation in metals occurs by DISLOCATION MOTION, not by simultaneous bond breaking. A wave of dislocations crosses the crystal; net result is shear.

**Theoretical vs actual yield strength**:
- Theoretical (slip entire planes at once): $\tau_{\text{th}} \sim G/10$ where $G$ is shear modulus.
- Actual (dislocation glide): $\tau \sim G/1000$. Three orders of magnitude lower.
- Difference: dislocations let crystals deform incrementally.

**Strengthening**: HINDER dislocations.
- **Solid-solution**: solute atoms pin dislocations.
- **Precipitation**: precipitates of second phase block dislocations (Al-Cu age hardening; superalloys).
- **Work hardening**: dislocations tangle into denser dislocation forests.
- **Grain boundaries**: dislocations can't easily cross grains.
- **Particle reinforcement**: hard particles obstruct.

All real engineering metals work via combinations of these strengthening mechanisms.

slides.title: Dislocations + slip systems
slides.body:
**Dislocation glide**: dislocation moves through crystal under applied stress, leaving net plastic deformation. Burgers vector = magnitude of slip per dislocation.

**Critical resolved shear stress (CRSS)**: applied stress, resolved onto slip plane + slip direction. Must exceed CRSS for dislocations to glide. CRSS varies by metal + temperature.

**Schmid's law**: $\tau = \sigma \cos\phi \cos\lambda$ where $\phi$ = angle to slip-plane normal, $\lambda$ = angle to slip direction.

**Slip systems**:
- **FCC**: {111} planes × <110> directions. 12 independent slip systems → high ductility.
- **BCC**: {110}, {112}, {123} × <111>. ~48 slip systems but higher Peierls stress at low T (BCC iron brittle below ~-40°C — Liberty Ships catastrophe).
- **HCP**: (0001) basal + <11̄20> directions. Only 3 slip systems. Low ductility at room T (Mg, Zn, Ti).

Von Mises criterion: need ≥5 INDEPENDENT slip systems for polycrystal ductility. FCC has 5; HCP doesn't → polycrystalline HCP metals are brittle unless engineered (Ti alloys with α+β microstructure).

**Dislocation interactions**:
- **Tangling**: parallel dislocations attract/repel; high density → forests → strong material.
- **Cross-slip**: screw dislocations switch planes. Allows recovery + ductility.
- **Climb**: edge dislocations move out-of-plane via vacancy diffusion. Requires high T → CREEP.

**Recovery + recrystallization**: heating an deformed metal:
1. **Recovery** (~0.3 $T_m$ in K): dislocations annihilate + rearrange into cells.
2. **Recrystallization** (~0.4-0.5 $T_m$): new strain-free grains nucleate + grow.
3. **Grain growth**: above recrystallization T, grains coarsen.

Used in industrial processing: cold-roll → anneal cycle → control microstructure + properties.

slides.title: Planar defects: grain boundaries + interfaces
slides.body:
**Grain boundary**: interface between two crystals of different orientation.

Real polycrystalline metals are made of MANY small crystals (grains), each ~µm-mm in size. Grain boundaries are 2D defects between them.

**Hall-Petch relation**: yield strength inversely proportional to square root of grain size.
$$\sigma_y = \sigma_0 + k / \sqrt{d}$$

Where $d$ = average grain diameter. Smaller grains = stronger. (Limit: nanocrystalline regime has inverse Hall-Petch behavior).

**Why**: grain boundaries impede dislocation motion. Each grain must accommodate plastic strain independently → harder for dislocations to flow.

**Grain refinement strategies**:
- **Solidification rate**: faster cooling → finer grains.
- **Mechanical work + recrystallization**: deformation + anneal → equiaxed fine grains.
- **Inoculants**: in casting, add particles that nucleate many small grains (Al-Ti-B in Al alloys).
- **Severe plastic deformation** (ECAP, HPT): produces submicron grains.

**Grain boundary character**:
- **Low-angle** (<15° misorientation): array of dislocations.
- **High-angle**: discrete interface, harder to characterize.
- **Twin boundary**: special case, mirror symmetry across boundary. Often coherent + low-energy. Common in FCC (annealing twins in copper) + Mg.
- **Coincidence Site Lattice (CSL)**: special boundaries with periodic atomic match. Lower energy + properties (corrosion resistance, crack propagation).

**Texture (preferred orientation)**: not all grains have random orientation. Rolled, drawn, extruded metals develop preferred orientations.
- **Sheet texture**: e.g., (200) in copper sheet.
- **Fiber texture**: e.g., <100> drawn wire.
- Affects formability, anisotropy, magnetic properties.

**3D defects**: voids, inclusions, precipitates.
- **Inclusions**: foreign particles (oxides, sulfides). Stress concentrators; often crack initiation sites.
- **Precipitates**: deliberate second-phase particles (Al₃Sc in aerospace Al; γ' in nickel superalloys). Strengthening.
- **Voids**: pores from solidification or accumulated vacancies under creep. Failure sites.

**Engineering microstructure**: the central concept. Choose alloy + process to get target microstructure (grain size, phases, precipitate distribution, texture). Properties FOLLOW from microstructure.

question.question: Apply Hall-Petch
question.goal: Steel: $\sigma_0 = 50$ MPa, $k = 0.7$ MPa·m^{1/2}. Yield strength at $d = 100$ μm vs $d = 1$ μm.

steps.reveal: $\sigma_y = 750$ MPa. 6× stronger than the 100 μm steel.

steps.prompt: How to achieve sub-micron grain size in practice?

options: Severe plastic deformation (Equal-Channel Angular Pressing, High-Pressure Torsion) imposes huge shear strain → ultra-fine grain microstructures. Or controlled thermomechanical processing (rolling + annealing cycles).

steps.reveal: Severe plastic deformation + controlled thermomechanical processing. Standard heat treatment can't reach sub-μm. ECAP, HPT, accumulative roll bonding etc. produce ultra-fine-grain (UFG) materials with dramatically higher strength.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\sigma_y = \sigma_0 + k / \sqrt{d}}$$ Hall-Petch is one of the most-used relations in metallurgy. Refining grain size from mm to μm to submicron grants huge strength gains. The strategy is universal across steels, aluminum, copper, titanium, magnesium. There IS a limit: at nm-scale, grain boundary sliding kicks in + materials get WEAKER (inverse Hall-Petch). Optimal grain size ~100 nm - 1 μm for many alloys.

question.question: Why is theoretical strength of metals (~G/10) ~1000× higher than what we measure?
options: Plastic deformation in metals occurs via DISLOCATION MOTION, not simultaneous breaking of all bonds in a plane. Dislocations let crystals deform incrementally at far lower stress. The gap between theoretical + actual yield is the fundamental observation that led to dislocation theory (1930s).
Materials are stronger than we think.
question.explanation: Pure shear of an entire atomic plane requires breaking many bonds at once → very high stress (~G/10 theoretically). Real crystals deform via dislocations: shear propagates as a wave through the lattice, breaking only a few bonds at a time. The gap between G/10 (theoretical) + measured G/1000 led Taylor, Orowan, Polanyi (1934 independently) to propose dislocations. Modern EM imaging directly visualizes them. All metal forming + strengthening engineering builds on this physics.

hints: Why is theoretical strength so high?
slides.workedSolution: Theoretical: shear an entire plane simultaneously → break all bonds across plane → very high stress (G/10). Actual: dislocations propagate, breaking bonds sequentially → far lower stress (G/1000). The discovery of dislocations in 1934 explained this. All metallurgical strengthening (cold-work, alloying, precipitates) operates by hindering dislocations. Theoretical strength is approached only in defect-free whiskers (single-crystal fibers) — relevant to whisker-reinforced composites.

Creep in turbine blades
question.prompt: Jet-engine turbine blades operate near material melting point + slowly elongate (creep). Walk through how dislocations + grain boundaries + precipitates + single-crystal casting all contribute to creep resistance.
Explain in two or three sentences why understanding defects is more important than understanding perfect crystals in real materials engineering.
question.rubric: Mentions that perfect crystals would be 1000× stronger but couldn't be processed/formed; properties like strength, ductility, conductivity, diffusion are DEFECT-CONTROLLED; engineering tunes defect populations (work hardening, precipitates, grain refinement) to achieve target properties; the entire metallurgy + ceramic + semiconductor industries rest on defect manipulation.
